summary: Profiles X.509 version 3 certificates and version 2 certificate revocation lists for use on the Internet. It narrows a broad international standard to what Internet applications need. It was a proposed standard, replaced by RFC 3280.

eli5.summary: A certificate is like an official ID card for a website or a person. This document says exactly which parts the ID card must have for use online.

subtitle: How to use digital certificates to prove identity on the internet.

tldr.problem: The internet needs a standard way for anyone to prove their identity and encrypt messages, but the X.509 standard is broad and complex.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2459 profiles X.509 version 3 certificates and version 2 certificate revocation lists, narrowing the international standard to what internet applications actually need, with clear rules for certificate structure, extensions, and validation.
tldr.outcome: This became the foundation for HTTPS, email security, and other internet security. It was replaced by RFC 3280 in 2002 with improvements and clearer specifications.

today: RFC 2459 was obsoleted by RFC 3280 in 2002, which refined the profile and clarified the validation algorithm. PKIX (Public Key Infrastructure X.509) work continues with newer RFCs that define protocols for managing certificates and validating paths. The architecture and core concepts described in RFC 2459 remain foundational to HTTPS, email security, code signing, and other internet security infrastructure.

sections.title: What Is a Digital Certificate?
sections.content:
A digital certificate is an electronic ID card that proves someone or something is who they claim to be. It contains the owner's name, a public key (a number used for encryption and verification), and a digital signature from a trusted authority called a Certification Authority or CA.

RFC 2459 defines how these certificates should be structured and what information they must contain. It also explains how to check that a certificate is real, and how to know when a certificate has been revoked (invalidated). The standard described here became the foundation for HTTPS websites, email encryption, and other internet security.
sections.eli5: A digital certificate is like a passport for a website or a person online. It has a picture (encoded as data), a name, and a signature from someone you trust that says the information is real.

sections.title: How the PKI Works
sections.content:
The Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is a system of four types of entities that work together. An End Entity is the user or website that needs a certificate. A Certification Authority (CA) is a trusted organization that issues and signs certificates. A Registration Authority (RA) is an optional middleman that helps the CA with paperwork and verification. A Repository is a database or website that stores and publishes certificates and revocation lists so anyone can find them.

When an end entity needs a certificate, they register with the CA (directly or through the RA), the CA verifies their identity, issues a signed certificate, and publishes it in the repository. Later, when someone receives that certificate (for example, when visiting a website), they can check that the CA signed it and that it has not been revoked.
sections.eli5: A CA is like a government office that issues ID cards. When you need an ID, you prove who you are, the office checks your proof, and issues a card they sign. The office also keeps a list of cancelled cards so people can check if your card is still valid.

sections.title: Certificate Structure and Extensions
sections.content:
Every certificate has several parts. The subject is who the certificate is for (the owner's name). The issuer is the CA that signed it. The public key is the number used to encrypt messages or check digital signatures. The serial number uniquely identifies the certificate. The validity period says when the certificate starts and stops being valid.

Certificates also contain extensions that add extra information. The key usage extension says what the key can be used for (signing, encryption, or both). The subject alternative name lists other names the owner goes by, such as email addresses or domain names. The basic constraints extension marks whether this is a CA certificate or an end-entity certificate. The certificate policies extension describes the rules the CA followed when issuing the certificate.

RFC 2459 specifies a required set of extensions and says which ones must be marked critical (meaning the software must understand them or reject the certificate).
sections.eli5: A certificate is like a passport with stamps. It has your name, a photo (your public key), and proof from the passport office. The stamps say what the passport is good for—travel, work, school—and when the passport expires.

sections.title: Revocation and Checking
sections.content:
A certificate may need to be revoked before its validity period ends. This happens if the owner's private key is stolen, if the owner leaves an organization, or if there is a mistake in the certificate. To announce revocations, the CA periodically publishes a Certificate Revocation List (CRL), a time-stamped, signed list of revoked certificate serial numbers.

When a system needs to verify a certificate, it not only checks the CA's signature and the validity dates, but also fetches a recent CRL and confirms that the certificate serial number is not on it. The meaning of "recent" depends on policy, but it is usually the most recently issued CRL. CAs typically issue new CRLs hourly, daily, or weekly.

RFC 2459 defines the structure of CRLs, including extensions such as the CRL number (to identify and order CRLs), the authority key identifier (to identify which CA issued the CRL), and the issuing distribution point (to say which certificates are covered by this CRL).
sections.eli5: A CRL is like a newspaper the government publishes listing cancelled passports. Before accepting someone's passport, you check the latest newspaper to make sure the passport is not on the cancelled list.

sections.title: Validation Paths and Trust
sections.content:
When verifying a certificate, the software must build a certification path, a chain of certificates starting with the certificate being verified and ending with a trusted root certificate. For example, the chain might be: your company's certificate (signed by your company's CA) → your company's CA certificate (signed by a larger CA) → the larger CA's certificate (trusted because it comes with the software).

RFC 2459 describes an algorithm for validating these paths. The software must check that each CA in the chain signed the next certificate correctly, that all validity periods overlap, and that the certificate is not revoked. It must also check the extensions, particularly the basic constraints (to verify that only CAs can sign other certificates) and policy extensions (to verify that the certificate was issued under an acceptable policy).

This architecture is more flexible than earlier systems such as PEM, which required a rigid hierarchy. With X.509 v3 extensions, different organizations can cross-certify each other, and software can determine which paths to trust automatically based on policy information in the certificates.
sections.eli5: Checking a certificate is like checking a chain of recommendations. If Alice says "I trust Bob because Carol approved him", you check if Carol's approval is real, and if you trust Carol. If both are true, you trust Bob.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 2459 specifies which cryptographic algorithms are allowed. For digital signatures, the standard supports RSA (a widely used public-key encryption method), DSA (a government standard), and combinations with hash functions such as MD5 and SHA-1 (both now considered weak). For keys themselves, RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and DSA are permitted.

The RFC does not require implementations to support any particular algorithm, but it specifies how conforming implementations must encode keys and signatures. This ensures that a certificate issued by one CA with RSA can be used by software from a different vendor that only knows how to use DSA (by validating with RSA and then using DSA for a different purpose).
sections.eli5: Signatures on certificates are made using math tricks. The RFC says which math tricks are OK and how to write down the results of each trick so different companies' software can read the signatures.
